message.content: I have heard indeed, around Naucratis of Egypt, that there was a certain one of the ancient Gods, to whom a bird is dedicated, which they call Ibis; but to the daemon himself the name Theuth. That this one first invented number and the computation of numbers, and geometry, and astronomy; again the game of knucklebones and of dice, and letters. There was then king of all Egypt Thamus, and in the most eminent and most ample city, which the Greeks call Egyptian Thebes; and the God himself they call Ammon. To this one Theuth, having set out, showed his arts, and said that they ought to be distributed next to the other Egyptians. But he asked what the utility of each would be; and, he himself reporting, what seemed well said, he approved indeed; what on the contrary, he censured. Where Thamus is reported to have shown to Theuth many things about any art whatever in each direction, of which, if we proceed to narrate the individual ones, the speech will be more prolix. But when they had come down to letters, "This discipline," said Theuth, "O king, will make the Egyptians wiser and more memorious. For this has been invented as a remedy of memory and of wisdom." But he said: "O most artful Theuth, one indeed is suitable for fabricating the works of an art, another more ready for judging what of advantage or of harm they are going to bring to those using. And yet you also, father of letters, on account of benevolence, have affirmed the contrary of what they are able to effect. For the use of them, on account of negligence of recollection, will produce forgetfulness in the mind of those learning; inasmuch as they, trusting in the external monuments of letters, will not revolve the things themselves within in the mind. Wherefore not of memory, but of commemoration, a remedy you have found. Of wisdom also the opinion rather than the truth you hand over to the disciples. For when they will have read through many things without the teaching of a teacher, experts of many [multaram: many? [?]] things in the common view, although they are ignorant, they will seem. In association also they will be more troublesome, as those who are not endowed with wisdom itself, but furnished with the opinion of wisdom."
message.reasoning:
I'm working through a literal, word-for-word English translation of Ficino's Latin passage about the Egyptian god Theuth near Naucratis, trying to preserve the original wording and sentence order as closely as possible.

Continuing this method, I'm rendering the lines about Theuth inventing number, computation, geometry, astronomy, the game of knucklebones and dice, and letters, keeping the awkward Latin syntax intact rather than smoothing it into natural English. I'm then translating the sentence about King Thamus ruling Egypt and the great city the Greeks call Thebes, associated with the god Ammon, noting the odd plural "quas" referring back to Thebes.

Next I'm working through Theuth presenting his arts to Thamus and arguing they should be shared with the rest of the Egyptians, followed by Thamus questioning the usefulness of each art—approving what seemed well-reasoned and criticizing what did not. I'm also translating the closing note that Thamus is said to have debated many points about each art in both directions, and that recounting them all individually would make the speech too long.

Then I move into the famous passage on writing: Theuth claims that letters will make the Egyptians wiser and improve their memory, calling it a remedy for memory and wisdom. Thamus counters that the inventor of an art isn't necessarily the best judge of its benefit or harm, and accuses Theuth, out of fondness for his invention, of claiming the opposite effect of what it will truly produce.

I note that reliance on writing will breed neglect of memory, since people will trust external marks rather than recalling things from within themselves, so what's really been invented is a remedy for reminding, not memory itself. Similarly, students will gain only the appearance of wisdom rather than true understanding, since they'll read widely without a teacher's guidance and feel knowledgeable without truly being so.
